supersede

/soo-per-SEED/ - rhymes with seed · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Supersede means to take the place of something older or less adequate.

The airline's new safety card supersedes the laminated one, though a few of the old sheets still lurk in seat pockets.

Example

On every ward, the 2024 dosing chart supersedes the 2016 edition — the retired chart went to the archive binder the same afternoon, not because it was wrong but because it was over.

Supersede is more precise than replace because it says the newer, authorized thing has made the older one obsolete — an orderly succession, with no force and no scheming about it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

displace: Displace means to push something out of its place or use — floods displace families, streaming displaced the video store — with no verdict on which thing is newer or better. Supersede adds order and legitimacy: the authorized newcomer takes over, and the old version is formally obsolete.

succeed: To succeed is to come after and take over in due course — the deputy succeeds the retiring chief, legitimately and on schedule. Supersede goes further: the newcomer does not merely follow the old one, it retires it, leaving the earlier version obsolete.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

precede: come before something

coexist: run alongside without replacing anything

Where it sits · how fully the old is replaced

patch → update → supersede

patch vs. supersede: A patch is far milder than supersede — one fix stitched onto the old thing, which soldiers on, while a superseded rule is retired outright by whatever replaces it.

update vs. supersede: Update is milder than supersede: an updated edition is still the same living thing made current, while a superseded one is retired outright by its successor.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — super-: above, over

Root — sede: to sit (Latin sedere)

Put it together: Super- (above) + sede (to sit, from Latin sedere) = to sit above — to take the seat of authority over what came before. The sitting root fills English: a session is literally a sitting, and sediment is what settles down. One famous quirk: because it keeps the Latin sedere, supersede is the only common English verb ending in -sede — spell it with an s, never a c.

Use the root in a new word: session: The court's morning session ran long, so the afternoon cases were heard by lamplight.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / bureaucratic

Supersede is the word of codes, standards, and editions: the new one takes over and the old one is formally obsolete, no elbows thrown. Supplant, taught in this unit, is its pushier twin — someone or something takes another's place, often by force or scheming. If a new rule supersedes the old, that is due process; if an adviser supplants a rival, watch your back.
